endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (b) all data used to train, validate, or operate the AI Technologies was lawfully obtained and used, and Service Provider has all necessary rights to such data;

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: (4) Ex ternal validation processes for ongoing evaluation of the model performance, e.g., accounting for AI model drift and degradation.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether requiring vendors to show evidence-constrained outputs and hallucination mitigation reduces inaccurate AI output reaching clinicians or patients, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The two endorsing sources address data rights and external validation rather than hallucination evidence specifically, so support for this recommendation rests on indirect expert guidance.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no comparative or observational test exists. The recommendation currently rests on expert endorsement alone, and the endorsements do not describe what counts as adequate vendor evidence.

The CHAI playbook text requires vendors to warrant that training, validation, and operating data were lawfully obtained. The augmented intelligence principles call for external validation that accounts for model drift and degradation. Neither quoted passage names hallucination or evidence-constrained output, so the recommendation extends these sources rather than restating them.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare procurement processes requiring vendor evidence of hallucination mitigation against processes that do not, measuring the rate of inaccurate outputs detected after deployment and any resulting patient harm. Work is also needed to define what form of vendor evidence, such as benchmark results, citation grounding tests, or independent audits, predicts accuracy in local use.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Vendor accuracy evidence drawn from other settings may not reflect error rates for patients who communicate in languages other than English or whose records differ from vendor test data, and health systems serving these groups may need local validation.
